title: A Full Vacuole Holds a Plant Up

scenes.tts: A cut stalk of celery can go limp and bendy. Put it in water, and it can turn crisp again. You drink water. A glass of water does not stiffen your body. A plant has no bones. So how does a plant stand up? And how are its cells different from yours?
scenes.visual: celery stalk droops, glass fills with water, stalk stands crisp; body block shows drinking water does not stiffen it; 'no bones'; two questions
scenes.narration: A cut stalk of celery can go limp and bendy. Put it in water, and it can turn crisp again. You drink water. A glass of water does not stiffen your body. A plant has no bones. So how does a plant stand up? And how are its cells different from yours?

scenes.tts: Plant cells and animal cells share many parts. A small part that has its own special jobs is called an organelle. The nucleus holds the cell's D N A, its instructions. The cell membrane is a thin outer layer. Mitochondria release energy from sugar, called glucose, in a form the cell can use. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like part. The endoplasmic reticulum is a folded network of membranes. A vacuole is a sac that stores water.
scenes.visual: animal cell and plant cell side by side; six shared parts are labelled in a centre column with leaders to both cells

The cytoplasm is the jelly-like part. The endoplasmic reticulum is a folded network of membranes. A vacuole is a sac that stores water.

The cytoplasm is the jelly-like part. The endoplasmic reticulum is a folded network of membranes. A vacuole is a sac that stores water.

scenes.tts: Plant cells add three more parts. The first is the cell wall. It is a stiff layer outside the cell membrane. It supports and protects the cell. Animal cells have no cell wall.
scenes.visual: a wall grows around the plant cell; animal cell marked 'no cell wall'
scenes.narration: Plant cells add three more parts. The first is the cell wall. It is a stiff layer outside the cell membrane. It supports and protects the cell. Animal cells have no cell wall.

scenes.tts: The second part is the chloroplast. Chloroplasts capture radiant energy and make sugar, called glucose. You find them in green cells. Plant cells still have mitochondria. So they can release energy from that sugar, day and night.
scenes.visual: plant cell zooms; chloroplasts appear; radiant energy arrows in; sugar dots travel to mitochondria
scenes.narration: The second part is the chloroplast. Chloroplasts capture radiant energy and make sugar, called glucose. You find them in green cells. Plant cells still have mitochondria. So they can release energy from that sugar, day and night.

scenes.tts: The third part is the large central vacuole. It is one big sac that fills most of a mature plant cell. It stores water. When water moves into the cell, the vacuole fills. A full vacuole presses out on the wall. The wall is stiff, so it pushes back. The cell gets firm. Many firm cells side by side make a firm stalk. When cells lose water, the vacuole shrinks, and the stalk goes limp.

A full vacuole presses out on the wall. The wall is stiff, so it pushes back. The cell gets firm. Many firm cells side by side make a firm stalk. When cells lose water, the vacuole shrinks, and the stalk goes limp.

scenes.tts: So how does a plant stand up without a skeleton? Its cells have stiff walls, and in soft parts, full vacuoles press on them. Your cells have no walls. Water inside them does not hold you up. Your skeleton of bones does. Plant cells add a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole.
